Guided Inquiry

Step 1 — Watch the geostationary satellite

The satellite is at h = 35,786 km, the textbook geostationary altitude. Watch the ground track (right panel) as time advances. Press Play if paused.

Notice: the sub-satellite point barely moves — the satellite hangs above one spot on Earth.

Step 2 — Predict: drop it 800 km lower

You are about to move the altitude to h = 34,986 km (800 km lower). What will the ground track do?

Step 3 — Observe the drift

The altitude has now dropped to 34,986 km. Watch the ground track: on every orbit the sub-satellite point steps a little further west. Read the drift per orbit in the sidebar.

The period is now less than one sidereal day, so the satellite completes each lap before the Earth has turned all the way under it.

Step 4 — The polar contrast

A polar orbit is deliberately the opposite: low altitude (~800 km), 90° inclination. The scene switches to a polar preset.

Watch the ground track: it is no longer a single point but stripes sweeping around the globe — a new patch of ground passes under the satellite on every lap. This is exactly what a weather or mapping satellite needs, and what a communications satellite must avoid.

Step 5 — The takeaway

Geostationary is a single solution. Kepler's third law fixes exactly one radius where T = 1 sidereal day: r ≈ 42,164 km from Earth's centre, i.e. h ≈ 35,786 km altitude.

Move off that altitude and the ground track drifts — westward if lower, eastward if higher. Polar orbits cover everywhere eventually; geostationary covers one place forever. Both exist for good reason.

Now explore freely: use the altitude, inclination and preset controls in the sidebar.

01

At a glance

A satellite goes round the Earth while the Earth turns underneath it. You set the height and the tilt of the orbit, and the sim draws the orbit, the satellite and the line it traces over the ground.

What you'll learn

  • How the height of an orbit sets the time for one lap.
  • What a ground track is, and how the turning Earth shapes it.
  • Why a TV satellite and a mapping satellite need different orbits.
The orbit is a ring around the Earth, tilted by i from the equator. The Earth turns about the dashed axis. Not to scale.

What's on screen

  • Earth, orbit, satellite: the globe in the middle, the orbit as a ring, and the satellite with its h label. The clock t is bottom right.
  • Home spot: the amber dot, a fixed point on the equator at longitude 0°.
  • Ground point: tick Ground track to open a world map. The green dot is the spot directly under the satellite, and its trail is the track.
See itPress the Geostationary preset and tick Ground track. Watch for: the satellite ringed by its h = 35,786 km label, the clock t counting hours, and a dashed ring around the amber home spot on the map.

Fixed: a circular orbit around a round Earth of radius R = 6371 km that turns once in a sidereal day. No air, no Moon, no Sun.

03

Gravity fixes one lap time for each height

Gravity alone keeps the satellite on a circular orbit, so GMm/r² = mv²/r. Here r = R + h is measured from the centre of the Earth, and μ = GM = 3.986 × 10¹⁴ m³/s². Writing the lap as T = 2πr/v gives Kepler's third law:

T = 2π√(r³/μ)  ⟹  T² ∝ r³
The satellite's own mass cancels.

A higher orbit has a longer path and a slower satellite, so the lap time grows faster than the radius.

Altitude hr = R + hSpeed vPeriod T
800 km7171 km7.456 km/s1.679 h
20,200 km26,571 km3.873 km/s11.973 h
35,786 km42,157 km3.075 km/s23.928 h
45,000 km51,371 km2.786 km/s32.187 h

The sim shows T but not v. From the first row to the last, r grows 7.16 times and T grows 19.2 times, which is 7.163/2.

See itSet Altitude h to 20,200 km. Watch for: Period T at 11.973 h, and the Earth shrinking in the frame as the ring grows.
04

The Earth turns once in a sidereal day, not 24 hours

A sidereal day is one full turn of the Earth against the stars: Tsid = 23.9345 h, which is 3.93 min short of 24 h, and the Earth turns 15.04° each hour. The ground track is the path of the point directly below the satellite. After one lap of T, the satellite has gone round 360° and the Earth has turned 360° × T/Tsid. The sim reports the mismatch as

Δλ = 360° (T/Tsid − 1)
Δλ is the Drift per orbit readout.

A lap shorter than Tsid gives a negative Δλ, and the satellite outruns the Earth. A longer lap gives a positive Δλ, and the satellite lags behind it.

Altitude hPeriod TT/TsidDrift Δλ
20,200 km11.973 h0.5003−179.91°
35,000 km23.262 h0.9719−10.11°
36,000 km24.111 h1.0074+2.65°
45,000 km32.187 h1.3448+124.13°
See itSet Altitude h to 35,000 km and tick Ground track. Watch for: Drift per orbit at −10.11° and Period T at 23.262 h, with the green dot leaving the amber home spot.
05

Only one height keeps the track still

Setting T = Tsid in Kepler's law leaves one radius, r = (μ Tsid²/4π²)1/3 = 42,164 km. With the sim's R = 6371 km that is h = 35,793 km. The familiar 35,786 km comes from R = 6378 km, so the preset sits 7 km below the sim's exact value and reads Drift −0.09°.

The orbit must also lie over the equator (i = 0°) and go the same way as the Earth turns. The satellite then stays above one point on the equator: it is geostationary. The sim labels a height as hanging still when T is within 0.05 h of Tsid, about 58 km either way.

Any other height drifts, and quickly: each extra 100 km of height adds about 1.28° to the drift per orbit.

Altitude hPeriod TDrift Δλ
34,986 km (800 km lower)23.250 h−10.29°
35,786 km (the preset)23.928 h−0.09°
35,793 km23.934 h0.00°
36,586 km (800 km higher)24.613 h+10.20°

The slider moves in 50 km steps, so it cannot reach 34,986 km. Use 35,000 km.

See itSet Altitude h to 45,000 km and tick Ground track. Watch for: Drift per orbit at +124.13° and Period T at 32.187 h, and the green dot leaving the home spot at once.
06

Tilting the orbit stretches the point into a figure of eight

The inclination i is the angle between the orbit plane and the equator. A tilted satellite spends half of each lap north of the equator and half south of it, so the latitude of the point below it swings between +i and −i.

At the geostationary height the period still equals Tsid, so the point comes back to the same place every day. But it no longer stays put. For i = 45° it climbs to 45° north, crosses the equator, drops to 45° south, and swings about 10° of longitude to each side of the home spot. The track is a narrow figure of eight, 90° tall and about 20° wide.

A small tilt gives a small figure: i = 10° moves the point by only 10° in latitude and 0.5° in longitude.

See itPress Geostationary, set Inclination i to 45°, and tick Ground track. Watch for: the track growing into a narrow figure of eight that reaches 45° north and south of the home spot.
07

A polar orbit scans the whole Earth in strips

At h = 800 km and i = 90° the satellite passes over both poles, with T = 1.679 h (100.7 min) and v = 7.456 km/s. In one sidereal day it makes 14.26 laps.

Each lap the Earth has turned 360° × 100.7 min/1436.1 min = 25.25° under the orbit. So the next track lies 25.25° of longitude to the west of the last, about 2800 km apart at the equator. Counting the climb and the descent, a day's laps cross the equator 28.5 times, which spreads tracks all the way round the globe.

At this height the Drift readout shows −334.75°, which is a whole turn less 25.25°. Read it as that 25.25° shift, not as a slow drift.

See itPress the Polar preset and tick Ground track. Watch for: stripes running from the top of the map to the bottom, each lap starting about 25° from the last, and Period T at 1.679 h.
08

Where it matters

  • Geostationary. TV, weather and communication satellites stay over one place, so a dish can be fixed. One such satellite sees about 42% of the Earth, up to latitude 81.3° north and south. A signal going up and down takes about 0.24 s.
  • Polar. Mapping and weather-imaging satellites need a new patch of ground on every lap, which is what the stripes give. They suit watching, not a fixed dish.
  • GPS. At 20,200 km one lap is about half a sidereal day, so the track repeats every day.
  • Real limits. The sim has no Sun or Moon, and no flattening of the Earth. Real geostationary satellites drift and need small thruster burns. Many real polar satellites are tilted a little past 90°.
09

Summary

In one line. The height and tilt of an orbit decide the path its ground track draws on the turning Earth.

Key points

  • T = 2π√(r³/μ), so a higher orbit takes longer for one lap.
  • Δλ = 360° (T/Tsid − 1) is zero only when T = Tsid = 23.9345 h.
  • Geostationary needs i = 0° and r = 42,164 km. The sim's preset reads −0.09° because it uses R = 6371 km.
  • The inclination i sets the latitude swing. A polar orbit at 800 km shifts 25.25° between laps.

Common mix-ups

  • "Any high orbit is geostationary." Only r = 42,164 km works. At 800 km lower the drift is already −10.29° per lap.
  • "A geostationary satellite is not moving." It goes round at 3.075 km/s. It keeps pace with the turning Earth, so it stays over one spot.
  • "The period must be 24 hours." The Earth turns once in 23.934 h against the stars, so that is the period needed.

Things to try on your own

  • Move Altitude h across the geostationary height in 50 km steps. Watch Drift per orbit pass through zero.
  • Use T² ∝ r³ and the 23.928 h at 35,786 km to predict T at 45,000 km. Then check it.
  • At 800 km, lower Inclination i from 90° and compare the stripes with the polar ones.
